title: Great Zimbabwe
summary: Great Zimbabwe, near Masvingo in southern Zimbabwe, was the stone-built capital of a Shona state from the 11th to the 15th century CE, a centre of the gold trade. Its Great Enclosure, an elliptical granite wall built in the 14th century, is the largest single ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa. The city was abandoned about 1450.

uncertainty.note: UNESCO says the property was built between 1100 and 1450 AD and founded in the 11th century; ICOMOS (1986) says the capital was abandoned in about 1450. The Great Enclosure itself dates to the 14th century (UNESCO).

where.historical_name: Great Zimbabwe, capital of a Shona state on the gold-rich plateaux; the Torwa and Mwene-Mutapa kingdoms later divided the region

importance.justification: The largest ancient stone structure in sub-Saharan Africa and the seat of a major gold-trading state, the site from which Zimbabwe takes its name.

footprint.description: The Great Enclosure is an ellipse of dry-laid cut granite south of the Hill Complex, about 250 m round and 88.5 m long, with a narrow passage between the outer wall and a second, unfinished inner wall leading to a conical tower. Only register figures from reference works and the ICOMOS evaluation were opened; no survey polygon.

phases.description: Great Enclosure built in the 14th century (UNESCO) of cut granite blocks in regular courses; the Hill Complex was inhabited from the 11th century.
The capital of a state extending over the gold-rich plateaux, with a population over 10,000 (ICOMOS), until it was abandoned.
Abandoned in about 1450, not through war but because the hinterland could no longer feed the city (ICOMOS); the walls stand as ruins and the site is a national monument.

materials.material: cut granite blocks laid in regular courses, with daga (granitic sand and clay) huts inside the enclosure

reviewer_note: Shape ring: the Great Enclosure, an ellipse not a circle (the plan dimension is the long axis of 88.5 m from EBSCO). Least sure of the wall height: the three opened sources disagree (ICOMOS 7 m, National Geographic Education over 9.7 m, EBSCO 11 m); ICOMOS is listed first as the heritage body, and the true maximum should be treated as uncertain. The Met Museum and Britannica pages (11 m, 252 m) were blocked, so not opened. The 1400 boundary between construction and intact is a round number inside the '14th century'. ICOMOS PDF text is OCR.
